title: Episode 326: George IV & William IV: The Prince Regent, the Royal Pavilion, the Sailor King, and the Great Reform Act of 1832
description:
The dramatic, contrasting reigns of King George IV and King William IV, the transition from Georgian extravagance to the modern era. George IV was the flamboyant 'First Gentleman of Europe': patron of Beau Brummell, builder of the exotic Brighton Pavilion and Windsor Castle, whose scandalous estrangement from Queen Caroline provoked riotous coronation scenes. Succeeded in 1830 by his eccentric, bluff younger brother William IV, the 'Sailor King' navigated intense constitutional crises to sign the landmark Great Reform Act of 1832, abolishing rotten boroughs and expanding the democratic franchise. Discover the last Hanoverian kings who bridged empire and modern democracy.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the two colorful brothers who reigned between George III and Queen Victoria: the decadent dandy of the Regency, George IV, and the bluff, unassuming Sailor King, William IV. Here is George with the extraordinary story of the Regency and the Great Reform Act.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: PRINNY AND BEAU BRUMMELL: THE REGENCY DANDY: 1762 TO 1820
Born in August 1762 at St. James's Palace, George Augustus Frederick, Prince of Wales—affectionately dubbed 'Prinny'—was endowed with brilliant charm, exquisite aesthetic taste, and an insatiable appetite for luxury, women, and debt. In 1785, George secretly and illegally married Maria Fitzherbert, a twice-widowed Roman Catholic, in violation of both the Act of Settlement and the Royal Marriages Act. Forced in 1795 to make an official royal marriage to clear his astronomical debts of six hundred thousand pounds, George wed his German cousin, Princess Caroline of Brunswick. The wedding was an unmitigated disaster: George was drunk at the altar, Caroline found him repulsive and smelling of brandy, and after fathering Princess Charlotte, the couple permanently separated in visceral hatred. Partnering with the arbiter of fashion, Beau Brummell, George set the tone for the Regency era: introducing tailored wool coats, immaculate linen neckties, and commissioning architect John Nash to transform London with the majestic curve of Regent Street, Regent's Park, and the breathtaking Indo-Saracenic fantasy palace of the Royal Pavilion at Brighton, adorned with minarets, domes, and Chinese dragons. George's obsession with sartorial perfection and court architecture drove the royal finances into perpetual chaos. Under Beau Brummell's exacting eye, the Prince Regent spent hours perfecting the knot of a starched cravat and introduced the revolutionary concept of daily bathing and understated elegance, replacing the heavy brocades and powdered wigs of the previous century. At Carlton House and Brighton, Prinny spent hundreds of thousands of pounds on French gilded furniture, Sevres porcelain, and Dutch Old Masters. Yet his private life was consumed by bitter recriminations: when his daughter Princess Charlotte died in childbirth in 1817, the British public openly blamed the Prince Regent for her tragic isolation, jeering his carriage whenever he ventured through the streets of London.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE QUEEN CAROLINE TRIAL AND THE BARRED ABBEY DOORS: 1820 TO 1821
When George III died in January 1820, fifty-seven-year-old George IV ascended the throne, determined that his estranged wife Caroline should never be queen. When Caroline returned from continental exile in June 1820, ecstatic crowds cheered her through the streets of London, viewing her as an innocent victim of a gluttonous royal tyrant. The government introduced the 'Pains and Penalties Bill' in the House of Lords to strip Caroline of her title and grant the King a divorce on grounds of adultery with her Italian courier, Bartolomeo Bergami. The trial was a public sensation: witnesses described bedroom keyholes and stains, but Caroline's defense, led by the brilliant orator Henry Brougham, turned public opinion into open revolt. The government was forced to drop the bill. On July 19, 1821, George IV celebrated the most extravagant coronation in British history at Westminster Abbey, costing an astronomical two hundred and forty thousand pounds. When Queen Caroline arrived at the Abbey doors demanding entrance, prize-fighters hired as royal guards physically barred her way and slammed the heavy oak doors in her face. Caroline died of fever three weeks later, broken-hearted. The Queen Caroline affair brought the British monarchy to the very edge of popular revolution. Radical reformers and working-class Londoners adopted Caroline as a folk hero, carrying banners through Westminster that proclaimed 'The Queen's Guards are the People's Friends!' During the House of Lords trial, Caroline arrived daily in an open carriage surrounded by cheering thousands, while George IV hid within Carlton House behind reinforced military pickets. Henry Brougham's closing speech for the defense was a tour de force of forensic rhetoric, warning the peers that destroying the Queen would topple the British throne itself. When Caroline was turned away from the Abbey coronation, she rode away sobbing in despair, her sudden death shortly thereafter prompting riots during her funeral procession through the East End.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: WINDSOR SECLUSION AND THE PASSING OF GEORGE IV: 1821 TO 1830
In August 1822, George IV made a historic state visit to Edinburgh, masterminded by Sir Walter Scott—the first reigning British monarch to visit Scotland since Charles II in 1650. Wearing bright royal Stuart tartan kilt over flesh-colored tights, George captivated Scottish society, popularizing tartan and reconciling the Highlands with the Hanoverian crown. Yet in his final years, George's immense obesity—his weight exceeding twenty-five stone—severe gout, and addiction to laudanum drove him into paranoid seclusion at Royal Lodge in Windsor Great Park. He conducted government business from his bed, wearing a greasy flannel dressing gown, signing state papers while hallucinating that he had personally commanded the cavalry charge at Waterloo. On June 26, 1830, sixty-seven-year-old King George IV died at Windsor Castle, his final whispered words to his page: 'My boy, this is death!' The Times published a devastating obituary: 'There never was an individual less regretted by his fellow-creatures than this deceased king.' During his Scottish triumph, George IV embraced the romantic Highland revival, sporting a bright Stuart tartan kilt, flesh-colored tights, and a Highland bonnet adorned with eagle feathers, completely winning over the Scottish clan chiefs who had fought against his great-grandfather at Culloden. Yet back at Windsor, George's final years were pathetic and reclusive: suffering from morbid obesity, chronic gout, edema, and arteriosclerosis, he spent his days in bed, sedated by massive doses of laudanum and cherry brandy. He communicated with his ministers from behind silk bed curtains, fantasizing that he had personally led the heavy cavalry charge at the Battle of Waterloo. When he expired in June 1830, the British public felt only collective relief, eager to turn the page on the decadent excesses of the Georgian era.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SAILOR KING: WILLIAM IV AND THE ROYAL NAVY: 1765 TO 1830
George IV was succeeded by his sixty-four-year-old brother, Prince William, Duke of Clarence, crowned King William IV. Known affectionately as the 'Sailor King', William was the complete antithesis of his decadent brother: bluff, plain-spoken, punctual, and unpretentious. Enlisted in the Royal Navy as a midshipman at age thirteen in 1779, William had served on active duty during the American Revolutionary War—where George Washington approved a covert plot to kidnap the young royal prince in New York City—and fought under Admiral Horatio Nelson in the West Indies, forming a lifelong friendship with the naval hero. For twenty years, William lived in domestic tranquility at Bushy Park with the celebrated Irish comedic actress Dorothea Jordan, fathering ten illegitimate children whom he affectionately acknowledged under the surname FitzClarence. In 1818, following the tragic death of Princess Charlotte, William married the gentle, pious German princess Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen. Ascending the throne in 1830, William dismissed George IV's French chefs, rode through London in an ordinary carriage, and insisted on a modest coronation. Prince William's fifty-year naval career had forged a blunt, hearty personality that stood in sharp contrast to George IV's effeminate dandyism. Having served under Admiral Horatio Nelson in the West Indies, William had survived storms, yellow fever, and open combat, rising through the ranks on his own merits. Nelson had famously praised William as 'the most attentive and dutiful officer I ever saw'. In domestic life, William lived happily for twenty years at Bushy House with the charming Irish comic actress Dorothea Jordan, fathering ten illegitimate children whom he acknowledged and loved with fierce devotion. When duty required him to marry Princess Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen in 1818, Adelaide embraced William's large brood with gentle maternal kindness, bringing calm, order, and sober domestic harmony to the eccentric royal sailor.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE CRISIS OF THE CENTURY: THE GREAT REFORM ACT OF 1832
William IV's seven-year reign was defined by the greatest constitutional crisis in modern British history: the struggle over the Great Reform Act. Britain's electoral system was an archaic medieval relic: rapidly expanding industrial cities like Manchester, Birmingham, and Leeds with hundreds of thousands of citizens had zero Members of Parliament, while uninhabited 'rotten boroughs' like Old Sarum—a grassy mound in Wiltshire with three houses—and Dunwich, which had literally washed into the North Sea, returned two MPs each, controlled by wealthy aristocrats. Led by Earl Grey, the Whig government introduced a sweeping Reform Bill to disenfranchise the rotten boroughs and extend the vote to the middle classes. In October 1831, when the Tory-dominated House of Lords rejected the bill, revolution threatened Britain: massive riots broke out in Bristol, Nottingham Castle was burned to the ground, and citizens threatened a general strike under the slogan: 'To stop the Duke, go for gold!' demanding the removal of the Duke of Wellington. The political system William IV inherited was an absurd, corrupt relic of the Middle Ages. Decayed villages known as 'rotten boroughs', such as Old Sarum—a windswept hill with no inhabitants—sent two members of Parliament to the House of Commons, while booming industrial powerhouses like Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, and Sheffield had zero parliamentary representation. When the House of Lords repeatedly rejected the Reform Bill, civil unrest exploded across England: the Bishop's Palace in Bristol was burned to the ground, rioters attacked Nottingham Castle, and prominent bankers organized a nationwide financial boycott against the Bank of England. William IV realized that without urgent electoral reform, Britain faced a catastrophic revolution far bloodier than France had suffered.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE KING AND THE CREATION OF PEERS: MAY 1832
In May 1832, during the tense 'Days of May', Earl Grey demanded that King William IV exercise the ultimate constitutional nuclear option: create eighty new hereditary Whig peers to swamp the Tory majority in the House of Lords and pass the bill. William hesitated, horrified at diluting the ancient peerage, and Grey's government resigned. William invited the Duke of Wellington to form a Tory government, but public fury was so explosive that Wellington informed the King that the army could not guarantee order if reform was blocked. William recalled Grey and reluctantly gave written consent to create the necessary peers. Faced with the royal threat of being swamped by dozens of new Whig lords, the Tory peers caved in and abstained. On June 7, 1832, King William IV gave royal assent to the Great Reform Act. The act disenfranchised fifty-six rotten boroughs, created sixty-seven new parliamentary constituencies for industrial cities, and increased the electorate by fifty percent, peacefully steering Britain away from violent revolution into the path of modern parliamentary democracy. The 'Days of May' in 1832 represented the greatest test of William IV's constitutional leadership. Facing the total breakdown of civil order and the threat of an armed march on London by the Birmingham Political Union, the King initially hesitated, reluctant to swamp the House of Lords with dozens of newly created Whig peers. But when the Duke of Wellington confessed that he could not form an alternative Tory administration nor guarantee that the army would fire upon civilian protesters, William capitulated. The King sent private circular letters to the Tory peers, commanding them to cease their obstruction and allow the Reform Act to pass. His decisive intervention preserved the hereditary House of Lords while peacefully opening the doors of Parliament to the industrial middle class.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SUNSET OF THE SAILOR KING AND THE PROMISE OF VICTORIA: 1837
In his final years, William IV governed with genial benevolence, abolishing slavery throughout the British Empire under the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 and overseeing the introduction of the Factory Act curbing child labor. His private obsession was living long enough to ensure his eighteen-year-old niece, Princess Victoria of Kent, could ascend the throne without a regency controlled by her manipulative mother, the Duchess of Kent, and her hated advisor, Sir John Conroy. At a grand birthday banquet at Windsor Castle in August 1836, with the Duchess sitting opposite, the seventy-one-year-old king stood up and boomed before a hundred stunned guests: 'I trust to God that my life may be spared for nine months longer... so that the royal authority may then jump into the hands of that young lady, the heir presumptive to the Crown, and not in the hands of a person now near me, who is surrounded by evil advisers!' Victoria burst into tears. William's prayer was answered: on May 24, 1837, Victoria celebrated her eighteenth birthday. Four weeks later, on June 20, 1837, seventy-one-year-old King William IV died peacefully at Windsor Castle, closing the Hanoverian era and ushering in the Victorian Age. William IV's final years witnessed a flurry of transformative legislation: the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 ended human bondage across the British Empire, while the Factory Act of 1833 placed the first legal limits on child labor in textile mills. William's overriding personal ambition in his final months was simply to survive until his niece, Princess Alexandrina Victoria, reached the legal age of majority at eighteen, thereby preventing her despised mother, the Duchess of Kent, from acting as regent. At a state banquet at Windsor, William publicly declared his fervent hope that God would spare his life so that Victoria might reign independently. He survived by less than a month past her eighteenth birthday, dying peacefully at Windsor on June 20, 1837, leaving the realm in honorable stability.
